title: William Gibson's "cyberspace"
hook: The author who named cyberspace wrote his novel on a manual typewriter.
peek: William Gibson coined the word cyberspace and imagined a world of hackers plugged into a vast data network. He wrote his novel Neuromancer on an old manual typewriter and knew little about how real computers worked.
lede: William Gibson's 1984 novel Neuromancer gave the world a vivid picture of cyberspace: a glowing network of data that hackers enter with their minds. It shaped how a generation imagined the internet. Gibson wrote it on an old manual typewriter, and he later said he knew very little about real computers when he did.

bullets.text: Gibson first used the word cyberspace in this 1982 short story. He later said he wanted a name that sounded exciting but meant nothing in particular, so he could fill it in as he went.
His picture of cyberspace came partly from watching teenagers in Vancouver arcades, hunched over the games. They seemed to want to reach through the screen into a space behind it.
In Neuromancer, Gibson describes cyberspace as a "consensual hallucination" shared by billions of users. The phrase is often quoted as one of the earliest pictures of a global network.
Gibson wrote the novel on a portable Hermes manual typewriter from the 1920s. He did not own a computer while writing it, and only bought one after the book came out.
The book was Gibson's first novel. It won the Hugo, Nebula and Philip K. Dick awards, a rare triple, and helped give the cyberpunk style its name.
